blocks.html: Q3 2025 was the Fund’s first active quarter following its official launch and we began by actively ramping exposure to CLO debt and shorter tenor CLO equity sourced primarily from the secondary market.
blocks.text: Q3 2025 was the Fund’s first active quarter following its official launch and we began by actively ramping exposure to CLO debt and shorter tenor CLO equity sourced primarily from the secondary market.

items: CLO Debt (73% of the Fund’s Exposure) – We purchased originally rated BB and single B CLO debt tranches at a weighted average price of $77.24 and 16.8% weighted average yield to maturity.5 These positions were predominantly from CLO transactions that have exited their respective reinvestment periods and where the manager is restricted from further trading. As we describe further in this letter, we believe this subset of the CLO investable universe represents an attractive opportunity given the limited buyer base.

CLO Equity (27% of the Fund’s Exposure)6 – Year to date, CLO equity has faced headwinds, with returns pressured by a sharp compression in loan spreads that has outpaced tightening in CLO liability spreads. While we see potential near-term catalysts for liability spread tightening as we highlight later in this letter, the challenging dynamic that has impacted the CLO equity asset class has also affected the Fund. 7

blocks.html: While longer CLO equity has generally appeared less compelling, we were able to identify select opportunities where relative value remained attractive for the Fund. One example of our discerning approach was a CLO equity position purchased in the secondary market on in July at a price of $28.375. In September, the deal was liquidated, which refers when the majority CLO equity investor directs the redemption of a CLO transaction prior to the stated maturity date and earns the excess proceeds of the market value of the collateral pool after paying back CLO liabilities at par. In the case of this transaction, we expect to receive liquidation proceeds that amount to nearly 10 points above our purchase price, highlighting what we believe is our ability to uncover compelling relative value even in a compressed spread environment.

blocks.html: Risk assets delivered positive returns across most asset classes in Q3 as trade tensions subsided, AI euphoria continued and the long-held expectations for the resumption of the easing cycle from the Federal Reserve came to fruition at the end of the quarter as the central bank finally joined the global rate cutting party and delivered its first 25 basis point rate cut since December of 2024. U.S. equity indexes reached new highs, bond markets were volatile but also saw gains as Treasury yields declined modestly at the ends of the curve, and credit remained resilient and well supported. The U.S. leveraged loan market also continued to perform well in Q3, buoyed by a strong technical with limited true new loan issuance that resulted in a meager 18% of Q3 issuance coming in the form of new money transactions. The market did hit a speedbump late in September as the sudden collapse of auto parts supplier First Brands Group weighed on performance in the final month of the quarter despite otherwise steady fundamentals. While not a top holding, First Brands was broadly held across CLO portfolios, and the swift plunge of its loans from the mid-90s at the start of September to the mid-30s before the eventual bankruptcy filing on September 29th.9

blocks.html: In our opinion, from the perspective of the CLO asset class, idiosyncratic defaults such as First Brands have consistently been expected to occur with some regularity ever since the CLO product was first introduced in the 1990s. We believe the CLO structure was originally designed to absorb these types of events. In other words, we believe this is not news, and the origination of the CLO product 30 years ago anticipated these events as a normal part of the credit cycle and created the CLO structure to withstand their impact. We believe much of the recent concern has been amplified by media coverage, which can overstate the significance of individual defaults. In our view, it is standard market practice - not unique to our approach - to anticipate such defaults as a regular occurrence throughout the life of a CLO which are fully incorporated into the underwriting process when calculating risk-adjusted returns. This is not the first such event, and we expect more to come in the form of credit losses that we have already budgeted for when structuring and underwriting securities. In J Fund, assuming a recovery rate of 30%, which aligns with the current quoted market price for First Brands, we estimate a credit loss of approximately 0.44% attributable to this event. For context, the Fund was constructed with the resilience to absorb up to 2.7% in credit losses under our base case scenario and 3.0% under our moderate stress scenario for the year 2025, underscoring our commitment to margin of safety. Beyond these stress budgets, we also budget for future ongoing credit losses from idiosyncratic defaults like First Brands throughout the life of the CLO, as part of our underwriting assumptions.10

blocks.html: We believe recent media coverage has materially misrepresented the risk profile of the CLO asset class. Unlike high-yield bonds, which are typically quoted and traded under a zero-default rate assumption, CLO debt is priced with a built-in annual default rate, typically 2%, applied consistently over the life of the deal. As we demonstrated above, our base case and stress analysis goes even further, incorporating conservative assumptions that include annual loss rates well above any historical precedent. Importantly, we do not view this scenario as a forecast, and it is a deliberate stress test designed to demonstrate the resilience of the structure and provide a margin of safety.

blocks.html: As a clear illustration of the structural durability that is frequently underestimated in the CLO asset class, year to date, the median par loss observed across the entire CLO universe has been 48 bps of par loss.11 If we were to include the loss incurred from the default of First Brands, this number increases to a median loss of 66 bps.11 This number is not only in line with the annual par loss observed over the last several years, more notably, this number is a fraction of our base and moderate case underwriting assumptions.11

Outlook12

blocks.html: We continue to believe an opportunity exists in a discrete subset of distressed CLO debt, many of which currently trade in the market in the price context of 50-80 cents on the dollar. We have identified a targeted list of distressed CLO securities that we have a unique angle on, whether through the underlying credit pool or the structural hidden nuances on the CLOs. Demand for CLO equity has been robust, supported by a deep and liquid secondary market. In contrast, in our view, distressed CLO debt - defined as originally rated BB or single B rated CLO tranches in aged CLO deals where ultimate impairment is likely - has limited demand with only a handful of investors equipped and mandated to analyze seasoned structures. We believe this imbalance has led to an inversion in relative value whereby distressed CLO BB and B tranches are trading at materially wider yields than CLO equity. At the deeply discounted levels at which we’ve been able to acquire our targeted positions, we believe these securities offer the potential for long-term returns in the 15–20% range, with a substantially greater margin of safety compared to CLO equity.131415

blocks.html: We believe the Fund is uniquely positioned to capitalize on this dislocation. Leveraging our credit research team’s deep expertise, we apply targeted stress scenarios to assess structural resilience and recovery potential. Our analysis reveals significant upside in this overlooked segment of the CLO universe. In our view, distressed CLO debt currently offers base case yields above greater than that of CLO equity, even after accounting for principal write downs. While CLO equity offers structural control in the form of the call option, we believe the yield premium in distressed debt presents a compelling risk-adjusted return. With only ~$3 billion in notional outstanding out of the $1.1 trillion outstanding CLO float, in our opinion this opportunity is both scarce and mispriced, but ideal for funds with the flexibility and expertise to allocate across the capital stack.

Potential Record of Maturing CLO Debt

blocks.html: We believe the technical backdrop is supportive of CLO liability spread tightening potentially due to a record amount of CLO projected to mature over the coming months. In Q3 2025, CLO liquidations, which is when a majority CLO equity investor directs the sale of the underlying CLO collateral pool prior to the stated maturity date and receives excess proceeds after CLO debt repayment, hit a record high driven by compressed equity cash flows from leveraged loan spread tightening. These liquidations have reduced overall CLO supply with AAA net supply forecasted to turn negative in Q4.16 It is our belief that our ability to source real-time data, while much of the market relies on CLO trustee reports that can be up to 45 days stale, enabled us to identify early that senior tranche amortizations were trending significantly higher than what a market standard 25% or even 30% annualized prepayment rate would suggest.17

We expect this dynamic to drive liability spread tightening, which we believe would benefit the Fund’s CLO equity positions, particularly those eligible for refinancing or resets at lower funding costs, as well as CLO debt.18
